nodes.details: The vulnerability is triggered when processing compressed data through the Snappy decompression routines.
The decompressor processes unvalidated compressed streams where length or offset fields may contain invalid values.
Parsed length and offset values can become negative due to sign extension, bypassing existing bounds checks and causing out-of-bounds memory access via unsafe operations.
The patch introduces explicit checks to reject negative length and offset values before they are used for memory operations.
The vulnerability is triggered during the processing of Zstandard compressed data frames, specifically when handling block checksums and final literal segments.
The issue arises when the decompressor processes malformed or truncated data streams provided by untrusted external sources.
Unsafe memory operations are performed without verifying that read and write offsets remain within the allocated buffer limits, causing out-of-bounds access.
The patch adds explicit boundary verification before reading checksums and copying final literals to prevent memory operations from exceeding allocated buffer sizes.
This method processes compressed data streams and directly manipulates memory buffers to perform decompression operations.
The vulnerability is triggered when processing specially crafted or corrupted LZO data that results in invalid length calculations.
The decompressor calculates match and literal lengths without validating their sign or ensuring they remain within allocated buffer limits before unsafe memory access.
The patch introduces explicit checks to reject negative length values and enforces strict input and output boundary limits before executing memory operations.
This function handles parallel decoding of four data streams and calculates memory offsets for processing.
The vulnerability is triggered when decompressing maliciously crafted or corrupted input that lacks proper structural validation.
Calculated stream start addresses are derived directly from unverified input data without checking if they remain within the allocated buffer limits.
The patch introduces a verification step to ensure calculated stream boundaries are strictly increasing and do not exceed the input limit before initialization.
The targeted function processes compressed data streams and performs direct memory operations to reconstruct the original output.
Feeding crafted input data triggers extended decoding loops that attempt to read beyond the allocated input buffer boundaries.

The implementation relies on low-level memory access primitives without verifying that read pointers remain within valid limits during variable-length token processing, causing out-of-bounds memory reads.
The update introduces explicit validation to ensure read pointers stay within allocated limits and detects integer overflow conditions before executing memory operations.
The method is invoked during HTML parsing to verify character set compatibility, triggering resource exhaustion when processing malformed markup.
The issue manifests when the parser encounters ill-formed HTML containing meta tags with specific character encodings that stress the compatibility verification logic.
Direct string-to-byte conversion without adequate error handling or bounds checking causes an out-of-memory exception during encoding compatibility verification.
The patch introduces a helper method with fallback logic to gracefully handle unsupported encoding operations, preventing crashes during compatibility checks.
The plugin writes authentication credentials directly to configuration files on the Jenkins master without encryption.
Attackers require Extended Read permission or direct file system access to the Jenkins master to read the configuration files.
The plugin implementation stores and processes raw password strings in configuration files and internal data structures without applying encryption.
The patch replaces raw string password handling with an encrypted secret object, ensuring credentials are properly masked and stored securely.
The vulnerability is triggered during the plugin's process of gathering server credentials to generate execution command lines.
The issue occurs when the Jenkins NeoLoad Plugin is configured with shared project or license server credentials, exposing them to users with Extended Read permission or master file system access.

The plugin previously handled passwords using plain String types without secure abstraction, causing cleartext credentials to be stored in configuration files and passed directly into command line arguments.

The patch replaces String-based password maps with Secret-based types and explicitly extracts plaintext only during the hashing process, ensuring credentials are properly abstracted and not directly exposed.
Serves as the initialization point where user credentials are accepted and assigned to the configuration object.
The plugin configuration accepts login passwords as standard strings, allowing them to be persisted without encryption.
Credentials are stored as plain text strings in the configuration object, causing them to be written unencrypted to XML configuration files on the Jenkins master.
The patch changes the login password parameter type from String to Secret, ensuring credentials are encrypted when persisted in configuration files.
The vulnerability involves the persistence of sensitive authentication data within plugin configuration files.
The plugin saves credentials in plaintext within global and job configuration files on the master node.
The implementation lacks cryptographic protection when writing credentials to disk, exposing them to unauthorized users.
The patch updates the object instantiation to pass a secret parameter, ensuring credentials are managed securely rather than stored in plaintext.
Handles global plugin configuration and processes server credentials.
Triggered when users apply global plugin settings through the Jenkins interface.
Passwords are persisted to the configuration file without adequate encryption.
Adjusts the configuration save logic to prevent storing credentials in plain text.
The constructor accepts the login password as a parameter and passes it to the parent class without applying encryption.
The plugin persists the login password directly in configuration files, allowing users with read access to view the plaintext credentials.
The password parameter is typed as a standard string, which causes the configuration system to serialize it without applying cryptographic protection.
The patch modifies the constructor parameter type to a secret wrapper, instructing the framework to automatically encrypt the credential during storage.
The class constructor and accessor methods directly handle the login password parameter.
Credentials are persisted in global and job configuration files on the Jenkins master.
The implementation stores and decodes the password as a standard string rather than utilizing secure encryption.
The patch replaces the string type with a dedicated secret class, removing manual decoding to ensure encrypted storage.
The plugin stores user credentials in global and job configuration files on the Jenkins master.
Users with Extended Read permission or direct file system access can read the master configuration files.
Credentials are saved in plaintext within configuration files instead of being encrypted.
The patch updates initialization to mock encrypted secret retrieval, reflecting a fix that ensures credentials are stored and accessed in an encrypted format.

nodes.CWE_ID_NAME: Plaintext Storage of a Password or Secret

nodes.details: The vulnerability is addressed within a test setup method that initializes mock objects for plugin configuration handling.
The plugin configuration and job files on the Jenkins master are accessible to users with extended read permissions or filesystem access. Sensitive data is written to these files without encryption.
The plugin fails to apply encryption mechanisms before saving credentials to configuration files, leaving them exposed in cleartext.
The patch modifies the initialization sequence to mock an encrypted value retrieval and inject a secret object into the constructor, enforcing encrypted credential handling.
The test setup method initializes mock objects required for validating plugin configuration behavior.
The plugin previously saved sensitive credentials in plaintext within global and job configuration files on the Jenkins master.
The implementation failed to apply encryption mechanisms before storing credential data in configuration files.
The patch updates the test setup to mock encrypted value retrieval, reflecting the remediation that ensures secrets are stored and accessed in encrypted form.
The setup method initializes test dependencies to verify secure credential handling mechanisms.
The plugin stores sensitive credentials in plaintext within configuration files on the Jenkins master prior to version 2.2.6.
Credentials are written to disk without encryption, allowing unauthorized users with read access to view them.
The patch configures a mock to return an encrypted value, ensuring the system correctly handles secured credentials during execution.
The plugin persists sensitive credentials directly within configuration files on the Jenkins master.
The vulnerability can be exploited by users possessing Extended Read permissions or direct file system access to the Jenkins master.
Credentials are written in plaintext to global configuration and job configuration files without encryption or secure masking.
The constructor is updated to accept a secure secret object, replacing hardcoded plaintext values to prevent unencrypted persistence.
The vulnerability targets the HTTP endpoint responsible for managing and deleting configuration files.
The affected endpoint does not restrict HTTP methods to POST, allowing attackers to initiate state-changing requests via cross-site forgery.
Individual endpoint handlers lacked proper authorization checks, and the centralized target method initially enforced insufficient access controls.
The patch removes redundant authorization calls from individual methods and enforces administrative access control within the target retrieval method.
The vulnerability targets HTTP endpoints responsible for validating and populating configuration file identifiers within the Jenkins plugin.
The endpoint fails to enforce POST-only request methods or validate cross-site request forgery tokens, allowing attackers to craft malicious requests.
The endpoint processes file ID requests without verifying whether the requester possesses the necessary project configuration permissions.
The patch introduces explicit permission checks to ensure that only authenticated users with project configuration rights can access the endpoint.
This method processes incoming HTTP requests to validate configuration file identifiers before creation or modification.
The affected HTTP endpoint previously accepted GET requests without enforcing POST-only submission, leaving it exposed to cross-site request forgery.
The handler failed to verify user permissions or enforce secure request methods, allowing attackers to delete configuration files via forged requests.
The patch introduces an explicit permission check at the start of the validation method to ensure only authorized users can access the endpoint.
This method generates a list of configuration file identifiers for Maven settings dropdowns.
The affected HTTP endpoint incorrectly accepts GET requests rather than requiring POST requests, facilitating cross-site request forgery attacks.
The handler fails to verify user permissions before processing requests, allowing unauthorized actions to proceed.
The update introduces a mandatory permission verification step to restrict endpoint access to authorized users.
This method serves as the primary entry point for the vulnerable HTTP endpoint that processes configuration file operations.
The endpoint accepts incoming requests without requiring the POST method, which enables cross-site request forgery attacks.
The handler fails to verify user permissions before processing requests, allowing unauthorized cross-origin execution of sensitive operations.
The patch introduces a permission verification step on the project context to ensure only authorized users can access the endpoint.
This endpoint processes user-provided API URIs to verify external service connectivity.
The method was accessible to users with minimal permissions and did not restrict HTTP request methods.
Accepting arbitrary URLs via GET requests without administrative verification enabled server-side and cross-site request forgery.
The update introduces a POST requirement and explicitly validates administrative permissions to block unauthorized requests.
This method serves as the HTTP endpoint for initiating the project shelving operation.
The endpoint processes state-changing requests without enforcing a specific HTTP method, allowing alternative methods to trigger the action.
The absence of HTTP method restrictions enables cross-site request forgery attacks by permitting malicious requests to execute privileged operations.
The patch introduces an HTTP method annotation to the handler, restricting execution to POST requests and mitigating cross-site request forgery.
Handles HTTP requests to unshelve or delete projects based on request parameters.
The endpoint processes state-changing operations without enforcing a specific HTTP method, allowing GET requests to trigger actions.
The absence of a POST requirement allows cross-site request forgery attacks to execute state-changing operations like shelving or deleting projects.
The patch adds a POST annotation to restrict the endpoint to POST requests only, mitigating CSRF risks.
The vulnerability is triggered when the server processes and stores connection identifiers in its internal registry.
The server relies on a hash table data structure to map connection identifiers to connection objects for management.
The connection identifier key class lacks robust hash code generation, allowing attackers to craft colliding identifiers that degrade hash table performance.
The patch replaces direct object instantiation with a factory method call to standardize key creation and mitigate hash collision exploitation.
This method is invoked during hash table operations for managing network connections, serving as the direct attack surface for hash collision exploitation.
Remote attackers can initiate connections using crafted identifiers that produce identical hash values when processed by the underlying hash table mechanism.
The method recalculates the hash code from the connection identifier array on every invocation, making it susceptible to deliberate collision generation and causing severe performance degradation.
The patch replaces the dynamic array-based hash calculation with a precomputed cached field, eliminating repeated computation and mitigating hash collision impacts.
The vulnerability is triggered during the deserialization phase when processing Java objects with custom property names and restricted setters.
The issue requires the mapper feature for inferring property mutators to be active, which causes the introspection logic to retain the backing field for write access.
The property renaming mechanism fails to drop the backing field mutator when the setter is explicitly ignored, allowing the deserializer to directly write to the field and bypass access restrictions.
The patch modifies the introspection logic to correctly strip non-visible field mutators when a setter is marked as ignored, ensuring the backing field remains unwritable during deserialization.
The method processes property metadata to apply explicit name overrides during deserialization setup.
The mapper feature for inferring property mutators is enabled by default, causing non-visible backing fields to be retained despite setter ignore annotations.
Renaming logic fails to strip inferred non-visible field mutators, allowing the deserializer to treat the backing field as writable and bypass ignore annotations.
The patch explicitly removes inferred non-visible field mutators from the property builder to ensure renamed properties with ignored setters remain strictly read-only.
The method processes findings and constructs the output structure containing vulnerability metadata.
The plugin processes vulnerability metadata extracted from Dependency-Check reports for display.
Vulnerability metadata is directly embedded into HTML and JSON structures without sanitization, allowing malicious payloads to be stored and executed.
The patch introduces an escaping function to sanitize all dependency and vulnerability fields before they are added to the output structure.
The vulnerability is triggered during the initialization of the document parser used to process incoming job descriptions.
The system processes externally provided job description files containing XML data without sufficient validation mechanisms.
The underlying XML parsing mechanism lacks proper restrictions on external entity resolution, facilitating injection attacks.
The patch adjusts the loop condition to strictly enforce the maximum retrieval limit, preventing an off-by-one boundary error.

nodes.details: The scheduler initialization process loads configuration properties and merges system properties into the configuration object.
The initialization routine retrieves system properties and directly merges them into the scheduler configuration without strict validation.
Using putAll to merge system properties lacks type checking and can cause concurrent modification exceptions or unintended configuration overrides.
The patch replaces putAll with explicit enumeration and type validation, using setProperty to safely merge system properties into the configuration.

nodes.CWE_ID_NAME: Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference

nodes.details: The method initializes the XML parser used to process incoming job description files.
The application processes external job description files without verifying their safety before parsing.
The XML parser factory is initialized without disabling external entity resolution or DTD handling.
The update configures the parser factory to explicitly block DOCTYPE declarations and prevent external DTD and entity loading.

nodes.CWE_ID_NAME: Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference

nodes.details: The vulnerability is triggered when the scheduler processes XML job descriptions.
The system accepts and parses external XML job descriptions without sufficient input validation.
The XML parser configuration permits the resolution of external entities, allowing XXE attacks.
The patch adds explicit case handling for all misfire policies and logs warnings for unrecognized values to ensure predictable schedule builder behavior.
The vulnerability occurs during the execution of the request processing pipeline within the authentication valve component.
An authenticated user initiates a request that traverses the valve chain before access control is enforced.
The system proceeds to invoke downstream components without first verifying the authorization status of the current response.
The patch introduces an immediate authorization verification step following the downstream invocation to block unauthorized access before further processing.
The method responsible for validating post-login redirect URLs before returning them to the authentication flow.
The authentication plugin processes user-supplied redirect URLs after successful OpenID Connect login.
The validation logic fails to strictly enforce domain matching, allowing attacker-controlled URLs to bypass legitimacy checks.
The patch modifies the method's access level to protected, enabling subclasses to override or extend the validation behavior.
This method handles the retrieval of system user authentication tokens through an external API client.
Authentication credentials are assembled using a builder pattern before being transmitted to an authentication service.
The password field is erroneously initialized with the username variable instead of the actual password variable, resulting in invalid authentication parameters.
The patch updates the parameter builder to correctly assign the intended password variable instead of the username variable during credential construction.
The vulnerability is triggered during the initialization of the system user account, which handles authentication setup for the data export module.
The module relies on pre-configured, unchanging authentication tokens or passwords during system user setup, bypassing dynamic authentication checks.
Hard-coded credentials are embedded within the FOLIO mod-data-export-spring module, enabling unauthenticated access to critical APIs and user data manipulation.
The patch introduces logic to properly revoke existing authentication credentials and issue new ones during system user preparation, eliminating reliance on static credentials.
The method handles the creation and credential setup for a system user during application startup or tenant initialization.
The vulnerability permits unauthenticated actors to interact with critical system APIs due to predictable authentication data.
The original implementation assigns a static, predictable value to the user password field during credential storage.
The patch removes conditional credential saving, enforces credential deletion before recreation, and replaces the static value with a dynamic parameter to ensure secure authentication.
The vulnerability mitigation is implemented at the initial execution point of the Spring Boot application. This ensures security checks occur before any services are initialized.
The application previously proceeded without verifying the presence of a required authentication environment variable. This allowed unauthenticated users to access critical system APIs.

The software relied on implicit or hard-coded authentication defaults instead of enforcing explicit credential validation. This design flaw permitted unauthorized access when configuration was absent.
The patch introduces a startup check that terminates execution if the required authentication environment variable is empty. This prevents the application from running without proper credentials.
The vulnerability is triggered during the initialization phase when the source reads and validates the provider URL configuration parameter.
The application must initialize a JMS source instance and provide a provider URL or connection factory name via configuration context.
The configuration process performs a JNDI lookup on the provided URL without adequate validation, enabling untrusted data to be deserialized and potentially leading to remote code execution.
The patch replaces inline URI validation logic with a centralized verification method to properly validate the provider URL and connection factory name before JNDI operations.
The constructor processes configuration parameters to establish a JMS connection and resolve the target destination.
The application accepts a destination name or provider URL from external configuration without verifying its safety before processing.
Performing an unvalidated JNDI lookup on untrusted input enables malicious object deserialization, leading to remote code execution.
The patch replaces a partial URI scheme check with a dedicated verification function to ensure the destination name is safe before lookup.
The vulnerability is triggered during the configuration and initialization phase of the JMS source component.
The JMSSource component accepts a providerUrl parameter that dictates the JNDI lookup target.
A JNDI lookup is executed on the provided URL without validating the protocol or content, enabling unsafe deserialization.
The patch introduces a system property to explicitly define and restrict allowed JNDI protocols, preventing unsafe lookups.
The vulnerability is triggered when the JMS source component is initialized with a custom provider URL.
The application permits configuring a JMS source with a provider URL that triggers a JNDI lookup operation.
The system executes a JNDI lookup on the supplied URL without validating the protocol, allowing untrusted data deserialization.
The fix restricts JNDI lookups to a safe protocol by setting a system property that only permits TCP connections.
The method attempts to establish a database connection and handles failures by logging exception details.
The vulnerability manifests when the database connection attempt fails, triggering the exception handling logic.
The exception handler directly passes the database properties object to the logging message, causing sensitive credentials to be printed in plaintext.
The patch replaces the direct database properties argument with a masked placeholder string to prevent sensitive information from being exposed in exception messages.
The request handler for fetching folder library settings is exploited to expose repository information.
Users possessing only read-level privileges can trigger the configuration retrieval process without proper authorization.
The folder iteration logic accessed library properties without validating user authorization for each parent folder.
The update introduces a boolean flag to conditionally enforce configuration permissions before accessing folder library data.
The method serves as a validation interface for library default versions, which is triggered during configuration checks.
The validation endpoint lacked a POST method restriction, allowing it to be invoked via standard GET requests without authentication barriers.
The absence of proper authorization controls enabled users with minimal read privileges to query the validation logic and extract repository content information.
The patch introduces a POST requirement annotation to the validation method, ensuring that only authorized POST requests can trigger the version checking logic.
The method processes incoming web requests to retrieve global library configurations for job execution.
Users with minimal Overall/Read permissions can trigger the endpoint to access sensitive repository metadata.
The implementation directly returns library configuration data without verifying the requesting user's authorization level.
The update adds a conditional check requiring elevated permissions before returning data, otherwise providing an empty collection.
The test case validates the escaping behavior of raw wiki syntax inputs, directly exercising the rendering engine's macro handling logic.
Users with edit permissions can insert wiki syntax containing HTML macro delimiters into document fields that support rendering.
The rendering output is included within HTML macros without properly neutralizing special delimiter characters, enabling macro closure and script injection.
The patch expands the escaping rules to cover additional macro syntax variations, including closing tags with spaces and partial open tags, as demonstrated by updated test assertions.
The vulnerability is triggered when user-supplied wiki syntax is processed by the XHTML printer during document rendering.
Editable document fields permit the insertion of wiki markup that is subsequently interpreted as raw HTML output.
The rendering logic fails to properly escape closing macro delimiters and their partial prefixes, enabling context termination and arbitrary script injection.

The update replaces targeted string replacement with a generalized mechanism that escapes multiple forbidden raw string prefixes and suffixes, including whitespace variations, to prevent macro injection.

nodes.CWE_ID_NAME: Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection')

nodes.details: This method constructs the filter chain resolver and applies security configurations, acting as the primary initialization point for URL filtering.
The system operates on a case-insensitive file system where mixed-case filenames resolve to the same resource.
The URL path matching logic performs strict case-sensitive comparisons, allowing capitalization variations to evade configured authentication rules.
The patch propagates a case-insensitivity flag to the filter chain manager and resolver, ensuring normalized path comparisons during request evaluation.
The vulnerability is triggered during URL filter chain resolution when request paths are evaluated against configured security rules.
The application runs on an operating system that treats filenames with different capitalization as identical, while filter rules use lower-case patterns.
The pattern matcher fails to account for filesystem case-insensitivity, allowing capitalization variations in requests to evade configured lower-case filter rules.
The patch adds override annotations to ensure proper interface implementation. This change facilitates the new configuration parameter that explicitly handles case-insensitive pattern matching.
The vulnerability is triggered during the initialization and application of filter chain configurations to specific URL paths.
The application runs on an operating system that treats mixed-case filenames as identical, such as macOS or Windows.
The filter chain manager does not propagate case-insensitivity settings to path configuration processors, allowing capitalization variations to bypass authentication rules.
The patch explicitly invokes a configuration setter to apply case-insensitivity parameters to the path config processor during filter initialization.
The path matching component processes URL patterns against request paths to determine access control rules.
The vulnerability manifests when the underlying operating system treats filenames with different capitalization as identical, such as on macOS or Windows.
The original implementation performs exact character matching without accounting for case differences, allowing attackers to bypass filters by varying filename capitalization.
The patch modifies character comparison logic to use a case-insensitive check, ensuring pattern matching aligns with case-insensitive filesystem behavior.
The vulnerability affects specific API endpoints responsible for adding or removing agent labels within the plugin.
Access to these endpoints previously only required a global Swarm secret, bypassing standard permission validations.
The implementation lacked role-based permission checks, allowing any authenticated user with basic agent creation rights to modify any agent's labels.
The patch removes the secret query parameter from the request construction, enforcing stricter permission requirements and POST method validation.
The client initialization process manages master discovery and authentication setup.
The system relies on a global secret for access without performing standard permission checks.
Sensitive authentication secrets are directly concatenated into log messages without sanitization.
The patch eliminates the secret variable from the connection log statement to prevent information disclosure.
The vulnerability pertains to API endpoints responsible for retrieving and modifying agent labels, which previously lacked proper access controls.
The affected endpoints relied exclusively on a global Swarm secret for authentication instead of enforcing standard permission checks.
The implementation failed to verify agent-specific configuration permissions, allowing users with minimal privileges to alter labels of any agent.
The patch eliminates the global secret parameter from the request URL, shifting authentication to POST methods and agent-specific permissions.
The vulnerability affects the API methods responsible for adding and removing labels to Jenkins agents.
Prior to the fix, the affected endpoints only validated requests against a global Swarm secret without enforcing standard Jenkins permission checks.
The code relied solely on a shared secret for authorization and lacked HTTP method restrictions, allowing unauthorized label modifications and cross-site request forgery.
The patch removes the global secret validation, adds POST request requirements, and introduces explicit permission checks for agent configuration.
The vulnerability targets the plugin's API endpoints used for managing agent labels.
Access to these endpoints was previously controlled solely by a global Swarm secret without additional permission verification.
The system failed to enforce agent-specific configuration permissions, enabling unauthorized label modifications by users with basic agent creation rights.
The patch eliminates the secret parameter from the candidate constructor to align with the removal of global secret usage for API authentication.
The API endpoint responsible for handling plugin removal operations was identified as the vulnerable entry point.
The system lacked mandatory permission verification for sensitive administrative actions before the update.
Attackers could arbitrarily remove plugins because the application failed to validate user privileges for critical operations.
The update introduces permission validation mechanisms to ensure only authorized administrators can execute plugin management functions.

nodes.details: The vulnerability is triggered during the XML transformation step in the post-build step when processing user-controlled input files.
An attacker must be able to supply or control the XML input file processed by the post-build step.
The transformer factory is instantiated without enabling secure processing, leaving it vulnerable to XML external entity injection.
The patch configures the transformer factory to enable secure processing, effectively disabling external entity resolution.

nodes.details: The vulnerability occurs when the application processes an external XSL stylesheet without enforcing security constraints on the underlying XML parser.
An attacker must control the input files provided to the post-build step to inject crafted XML containing external entities.
The XML processing component is initialized without enabling secure processing, allowing external entity resolution during stylesheet compilation.
The update configures the XML processor to enforce secure processing, thereby disabling external entity resolution to prevent injection attacks.

nodes.details: The vulnerability is triggered during the deserialization process handled by the SOFA Hessian protocol.
An attacker must utilize a gadget chain that relies exclusively on JDK classes without third-party dependencies to bypass protections.
The existing blacklist mechanism fails to restrict specific JDK-based classes, allowing a gadget chain to bypass deserialization security controls.
The vulnerability is resolved by expanding the serialization blacklist to explicitly block the identified bypassing gadget classes.
The vulnerability is triggered within the createSVNAuthentication method of the Subversion plugin's credential descriptor classes when processing SSH keys, SSL certificates, or passwords.
Credentials such as passwords and SSH private keys are persisted in configuration files using weak base64 encoding instead of secure encryption.
The code directly passes raw or base64-encoded credential strings to authentication constructors without applying proper cryptographic protection or secure secret handling.
The patch replaces direct credential access with secure wrapper methods like Secret.toString and getPassword to ensure proper encryption and safe retrieval of sensitive data.
The method processes client hints data to update and improve user agent information.
The vulnerability is triggered only when applications utilize the client hints analysis feature introduced in version 7.0.0.
The code accesses array elements derived from split version strings without verifying their length, causing an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException when the input data lacks expected components.
The patch refactors the version handling logic to safely parse version strings, validates array bounds before element access, and implements robust version comparison mechanisms.
Handles configuration updates for namespaces and orchestrates permission validation before executing synchronization operations.
Attackers can submit specially crafted requests to the synchronization feature to manipulate the target namespace list and bypass standard access controls.
The initial validation logic fails to verify that the target namespaces align with the authorized application and namespace context, allowing permission checks to be circumvented.
The patch introduces an additional validation step to ensure the synchronized namespaces are legitimate before proceeding with permission verification and configuration updates.
The vulnerability is triggered during the database authentication handshake when a plugin transmits credentials without transport encryption.
The driver permits authentication plugins that send passwords in cleartext to operate over plain TCP connections without verifying transport security.
The authentication plugin interface lacks a mechanism to declare a requirement for secure transport, allowing cleartext plugins to execute regardless of connection encryption status.
The patch updates the connection configuration to explicitly require an SSL mode, ensuring that clear-text authentication plugins are only permitted over encrypted channels.
The entrypoint configures the Active Directory security realm during system setup.
The Jenkins controller is configured to communicate with Active Directory servers without enforcing data encryption.
The security realm constructor is initialized with a configuration parameter that leaves data transmission unencrypted.
The patch updates the security realm constructor parameter to enforce encryption for data exchanged between the controller and Active Directory.
The vulnerability manifests when the Active Directory security realm is instantiated and configured with domain connection parameters.
The plugin initializes the Active Directory domain connection without mandating secure communication channels by default.
The security realm constructor lacks a built-in mechanism to enforce encrypted data transmission between the controller and Active Directory servers.
The patch modifies the security realm constructor call to include a new boolean parameter that explicitly controls encryption settings.
The plugin processes user and group credentials against an Active Directory server.
The authentication mechanism defaults to non-TLS connection flags when TLS requirements are not explicitly configured.
The directory service binding function is invoked with legacy flags that allow unencrypted network traffic.
The patch replaces static flags with dynamic configuration logic that defaults to TLS-enforcing constants when required.
The vulnerability is triggered during the configuration of the Active Directory security realm within the Jenkins controller setup process.
Jenkins Active Directory Plugin versions 2.25 and earlier default to allowing unencrypted communication channels between the controller and domain servers.
The security realm constructor lacks a default mechanism to mandate encrypted transmission protocols, permitting cleartext data exchange.
The patch modifies the security realm constructor to accept an additional boolean flag that explicitly controls and enforces encrypted transmission settings.
The vulnerability occurs during the LDAP bind operation used for Active Directory authentication.
The plugin defaults to unencrypted LDAP connections when the encryption flag is not explicitly enabled.
The code relies on a static configuration flag that fails to mandate secure transport for sensitive authentication data.
The patch replaces the static flag with a configurable boolean parameter to explicitly require TLS for all LDAP connections.
Serves as the entry point for testing and validating directory connectivity and credentials.
Data transmission between the controller and directory servers lacks encryption in default configurations.
The authentication provider initialization omits the security realm parameter, preventing proper TLS enforcement.
The modification passes the security realm instance to the provider constructor to enable secure communication.
The renderTemplate method processes Groovy templates for email notifications, acting as the execution point where the vulnerability manifests.
The vulnerability requires an attacker to have permissions to define or modify email templates within a Jenkins folder.

The server fails to perform access control list checks when a persistent watcher is triggered, allowing unauthorized path disclosure.

The server fails to validate access control lists when triggering persistent watcher events, leading to unauthorized path exposure.

The vulnerability manifests during the processing of watch events triggered by persistent watchers on accessible parent nodes.
An attacker must already possess access permissions to a parent znode to successfully attach a persistent watcher and trigger the subsequent event processing.
The server fails to perform an access control list check when the persistent watcher is triggered, allowing unauthorized exposure of child znode paths.
The patch modifies the event processing method signature to include an ACL list parameter, enabling the server to verify permissions before exposing znode paths.
Handles HTTP requests to validate external service connectivity using provided credentials.

The update introduces an HTTP POST annotation and explicitly verifies administrative privileges before processing the request to mitigate CSRF and unauthorized access.

Using the magic constant as the password incorrectly triggers authentication, allowing attackers to log in as any user.
The patch wraps the raw password in a dedicated password object to properly distinguish authentication from lookup, removing the magic constant reliance.
The vulnerability is triggered during the user lookup and authentication process within the Active Directory plugin's LDAP-based mode.
The LDAP-based authentication mode shares code for user lookup and authentication, relying on a magic constant to differentiate between the two operations.

nodes.details: The patch replaces the string-based magic constant with a dedicated password interface, properly separating lookup and authentication logic while redacting stored credentials.

The plugin historically used a magic constant instead of a real password to differentiate between user lookup and authentication operations.
Authentication logic failed to properly validate or distinguish between legitimate passwords and the magic constant, allowing unauthorized access.
The patch replaces the magic constant approach with explicit password checks and proper credential handling to prevent unauthorized access.
The method's return type was modified to address the authentication bypass vulnerability.

The patch changes the cache key type from a generic string to a dedicated CacheKey class to enforce proper separation.

The system relies on a hardcoded magic constant to represent missing passwords during remember-me processing or user lookups. This behavior is present in plugin versions prior to the specified fixes.
The authentication mechanism incorrectly validates the magic constant as a legitimate password, allowing attackers to impersonate any user by supplying it during login.
The patch substitutes the conditional dummy password with a fixed, non-guessable placeholder to eliminate the predictable magic constant used for credential-less lookups.
The vulnerability is triggered when processing untrusted JSON input through the readValue method.

An incomplete fix for a previous vulnerability leaves the type-checking blacklist bypassable by malicious JSON payloads.
The patch renames the test method to better align with its purpose of validating illegal type deserialization.
The vulnerability is triggered when processing maliciously crafted JSON input through this method.
The presence of Spring libraries in the classpath renders the existing type blacklist ineffective, enabling exploitation.
The original security check relied on a static blacklist of class names that could be bypassed, allowing unsafe deserialization.
The patch replaces the simple blacklist check with a dedicated subtype validation mechanism to enforce stricter type checking.
The vulnerability is triggered during the deserialization of JSON arrays into primitive types or wrapped values when the parser processes array tokens.
The issue only occurs when the DeserializationFeature.UNWRAP_SINGLE_VALUE_ARRAYS configuration is explicitly enabled, allowing single-element arrays to be unwrapped into scalar values.
The deserialization methods fail to verify if the next token after unwrapping is another array, leading to unbounded recursion and resource exhaustion.
The patch introduces a conditional check for the START_ARRAY token after advancing the parser, routing nested arrays to a dedicated handler to halt recursive processing.
The vulnerability is triggered during the deserialization of JSON arrays into Java objects, specifically within the logic that processes array inputs.
The issue only manifests when the single-value array unwrapping feature is explicitly enabled, which directs execution to the vulnerable code path.
The deserialization logic fails to validate whether the unwrapped value contains another nested array, allowing unbounded recursion and resource exhaustion.
The patch introduces a validation step to detect additional array tokens after unwrapping, immediately rejecting deeply nested structures to prevent unbounded processing.
The eval method processes user-provided parameters and executes sandboxed scripts, returning their results to the application.
The vulnerability manifests when sandboxed scripts return List or Map data structures for Reactive Reference Parameters without adequate output encoding.
The original implementation only applied HTML escaping to CharSequence return values, leaving List and Map types unescaped and vulnerable to stored cross-site scripting.
The patch removes the CharSequence type restriction and applies a dedicated sanitization function to all script return values when executed in sandbox mode.
The vulnerability manifests during the lifecycle management of the Seti component when internal channels are initialized and listeners are attached.
Remote clients can establish connections to the server and attempt to interact with internal Oort and Seti channels.

The update registers a global channel filter and applies channel protection during startup, while removing the filter and unprotecting channels during shutdown to enforce access restrictions.
The vulnerability is triggered during the startup phase when internal communication channels are configured and registered with the messaging framework.
Internal Oort and Seti channels are initialized without adequate access restrictions, leaving them exposed to external network traffic.
The channel configuration applies a blanket authorization policy that grants all users unrestricted subscription and publishing rights, bypassing intended security boundaries.
The patch removes the unrestricted authorization grant and replaces it with a dedicated filtering mechanism and dedicated protection methods to properly restrict remote access to internal channels.
The method delegates authorization checks to determine if a subject possesses the required access rights for a specific resource.
Resources are structured in a parent-child hierarchy where accessibility of nested elements depends on the permissions of their ancestors.
The authorization logic only evaluated permissions on the target resource itself, ignoring whether the user had access to parent containers in the hierarchy.
The update introduces a validation step that verifies the parent resource possesses the required read or discover permissions before granting access to the child resource.
The vulnerability is triggered during JSON deserialization when the polymorphic type validator processes array types, allowing bypass of security controls.
The application configures the type validator to automatically permit array types based solely on a configuration flag without inspecting their contents.
The validation logic only verifies the array flag and skips recursive inspection of the innermost component type, allowing non-allowlisted concrete classes to be instantiated.
The patch updates the validation method to recursively unwrap nested arrays and explicitly validate the innermost element type against the configured allowlist.
The application provides a method to parse incoming XML strings into Java objects without initial security validation.

The update introduces an XML input factory that explicitly disables external entity support before parsing the input stream.

This routine handles object transformation during unmarshalling, acting as the primary execution path where manipulated input streams trigger the vulnerability.
The vulnerability requires crafted input containing highly recursive collection or map structures that exploit hash code calculations during data processing.

An attacker must supply a maliciously crafted input stream containing highly recursive data structures that exploit collection hash code implementations during deserialization.
Adding elements to standard hash-based collections triggers exponential time complexity due to recursive structure collisions, leading to complete CPU exhaustion.
The patch introduces timing checks around collection element insertion to accumulate execution time and abort processing if a predefined threshold is exceeded.
This method handles the unmarshalling and insertion of elements into collections, serving as the direct execution path for the vulnerability.
The vulnerability requires processing input containing highly recursive object graphs or collections that exploit hash code implementations to force exponential calculation times.

The vulnerability requires processing input containing highly recursive collection or map structures that exploit hash code implementations in affected Java runtime types.
